title: One request. One clear ticket.
text: An errand should not become another project. Orange starts with a conversation, and turns it into one clear service ticket. The important distinction is simple: asking for something is not the same as approving it. You stay in control of exactly what happens next.

title: Start with what you need.
text: Let's find a plumber in Indiranagar for tomorrow morning, under fifteen hundred rupees. As the request arrives, the details settle into the ticket. The assistant keeps the service, location, time and budget together, so the conversation has a visible, editable source of truth.

title: Change one detail. Keep the rest.
text: Suppose the budget changes to twelve hundred. We can edit just that field. Everything else stays intact. Notice that the ticket stays in the same place, while the updated options appear inside the conversation. There is no page jump and no need to start the request again.

title: Reviews are information, not instructions.
text: These are local mock professionals, with prices and available times. One review deliberately contains an instruction to ignore approval and book immediately. It is displayed as provider text, but it cannot grant permission or change the request. The application enforces that boundary in code, rather than hoping a prompt will hold.

title: A quote becomes a review.
text: Choosing an option creates a temporary hold, not a booking. The ticket now shows the professional, date, time, and exact quoted price. These details are bound to the approval. If the provider, slot, or price changes, the old approval no longer applies. Nothing is booked yet.

title: A difficult case, on purpose.
text: Now let's make the provider time out after it has already accepted the booking. Activity opens in the same pane, with the conversation still beside it. We can review the exact action here and approve it once. The response will test what the agent does when the outcome is uncertain.

title: Check the result before claiming success.
text: The booking call returned a timeout. Instead of trying a new booking, the agent checked the authoritative booking status using the same operation key. That check confirmed the original booking. Only then did the ticket become a receipt. The price remains visible, and the trace shows how the result was verified.

title: A repeated yes is still one booking.
text: What if we confirm again, or reload the page? We still have one booking. The operation and its result are stored in SQLite, so a repeated confirmation reuses the existing result. Separate automated tests also interrupt execution after a provider commit and reopen the engine to verify recovery.

title: Changes get their own approval.
text: Cancelling is a new action, with its own review. Preparing it leaves the appointment untouched. After confirmation, the first provider call returns a temporary error. A bounded retry uses the same key and completes the cancellation. The receipt and activity log both reflect the actual result.

title: Memory you can inspect and change.
text: Preferences are just as explicit. We can save an area, see that it was stated by the user, correct it, or forget it. Inferred preferences require confirmation before reuse. Forgetting removes the saved fact and any inherited active context, rather than merely hiding a row in the interface.

title: Less to coordinate. More you can trust.
text: The result is a small, local application with a practical boundary between intent, permission, and completion. The interface stays anchored, motion explains the changes, and every outcome has evidence behind it. No real provider, payment, or model API is needed to run the app or its evaluations.
